Linear Algebra for Data Science

  • Data often come in tabular form
  • Linear algebra provides tools to manipulate and analyze such data efficiently
  • Many data analysis and solutions can be expressed using linear algebra
  • Software libraries (e.g., NumPy, R, MATLAB) optimize matrix operations for performance
    • NVIDIA CUDA has cuBLAS for GPU-accelerated linear algebra
    • Intel MKL optimizes linear algebra on Intel CPUs
    • Google XLA for optimizing linear algebra computations in TensorFlow
  • Understanding linear algebra is essential for effective data science

Single Factor Representation of Data

  • Recall the IQ model for student test scores: i.e., \(\hat x_i = q_i v,\) \[\mathbf{x}_{i \cdot}=\begin{pmatrix}x_{i 1}& x_{i 2} & \dots & x_{i 5}\end{pmatrix},\ \mathbf{v} = \begin{pmatrix} v_1 & v_2 & \cdots & v_5 \end{pmatrix}'\] where student \(i\)’s test scores \(\mathbf{x}_{i \cdot}\) is \(\mathbf{v}\) scaled by \(q_i\).
  • Matrix form: for \(n\) students, \(\mathbf{q} = \begin{pmatrix} q_1 & \cdots & q_n \end{pmatrix}'\). \[ \mathbf{X} \stackrel{?}{=} \mathbf{q}\mathbf{v}^\top = \begin{pmatrix} q_1 \\ \vdots \\ q_n \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} v_1 & \cdots & v_5 \end{pmatrix} \]
  • If \(\mathbf{X} \approx \mathbf{q}\mathbf{v}^\top\), then single factor model is approximately correct.1

Multiple Factor Representation

  • What if single factor model is not sufficient?
  • Extend to multiple factors (e.g., \(k=2\)):
    • Vector \(\mathbf{q}\) becomes matrix \(\mathbf{Q}\) of size \(n \times k\)
    • Vector \(\mathbf{v}\) becomes matrix \(\mathbf{V}\) of size \(n \times k\) \[ \mathbf{X} \stackrel{?}{=} \mathbf{Q}\mathbf{V}^\top \]
  • What is the maximum \(k\) possible?
  • If maximum \(k\) is used, is the approximation exact?

Rank-\(k\) Approximation of Test Scores Data

Code 
library(bootstrap)
data(scor)

pc <- prcomp(scor, scale = FALSE, center = TRUE)  # PCA

pc_approx_scor <- function(pc, num_pcs = 1) {
  Q = pc$x[,1:num_pcs, drop=FALSE]        # first PC scores
  V = pc$rotation[,1:num_pcs, drop=FALSE] # first PC loadings
  mu = pc$center              # variable means

  scor_hat = Q %*% t(V)
  scor_hat = sweep(scor_hat, 2, mu, "+")

  return(scor_hat)
}

hat_scor_1 = pc_approx_scor(pc, num_pcs = 1)
hat_scor_5 = pc_approx_scor(pc, num_pcs = 5)

# heatmaps: original scor vs rank-1 approximation
cols <- colorRampPalette(c("navy", "white", "firebrick3"))(100)
zmin <- min(c(as.matrix(scor), as.matrix(hat_scor_1), as.matrix(hat_scor_5)))
zmax <- max(c(as.matrix(scor), as.matrix(hat_scor_1), as.matrix(hat_scor_5)))

plot_heat <- function(mat, main = "") {
  m <- as.matrix(mat)
  image(1:ncol(m), 1:nrow(m), t(apply(m, 2, rev)),
        col = cols, axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
        main = main, zlim = c(zmin, zmax))
  axis(1, at = 1:ncol(m), labels = colnames(m), las = 2)
  axis(2, at = 1:nrow(m), labels = rev(rownames(m)), las = 2)
  box()
}
  
plot_heat(scor, "Original scor")
plot_heat(hat_scor_1, "Rank-1 approximation (hat_scor_1)")
plot_heat(hat_scor_5, "Rank-5 approximation (hat_scor_5)")

Matrix Factorization as Representation Learning

  • If data matrix \(X\) has \(n\) samples and \(p\) features,
  • PCA: \(X = Q_V V^\top\), where \(V\) has orthonormal columns
  • ICA: \(X = Q_W W^\top\), where \(W\) has “independent” columns
  • NMF: \(X = Q_Y Y^\top\), where \(Q_Y\) and \(Y\) are non-negative matrices
  • Bases, \(V\), \(W\), and \(Y\), are calculated by imposing different characteristics.
  • Each can be viewed as representation learning method.
  • Choice of method depends on data characteristics and analysis goals
  • Sometimes observations are columns and variables are rows

Representation Learning in Data Science

  • PCA rotates the data to compute transformed features
  • Other non-linear methods: t-SNE and UMAP
  • Similar goals: find lower-dimensional subspace representation of high-dimensional data
  • Start with a suitable representation (basis vectors) for the data

. . .

  • Linear algebra is fundamental for understanding and implementing these techniques
  • Bases, dimensions, subspaces, etc., are key concepts/terminology in linear algebra
  • Motivates review of linear algebra for data science applications

Linear Algebra Definitions

Definition: Subspace

A subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty subset \(\varnothing \neq V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) that satisfies

  1. for every \(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in V\), the sum \(\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w} \in V\), and
  2. for every \(\mathbf{v} \in V\) and every \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), the scalar product \(c \mathbf{v} \in V\).

. . .

Definition 1.4: Linear Combination

Let \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k \in \mathbb{R}^n\). A sum of the form

\[ c_1 \mathbf{v}_1+c_2 \mathbf{v}_2+\cdots+c_k \mathbf{v}_k=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i \mathbf{v}_i, \]

where the coefficients \(c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_k \in \mathbb{R}\) are any scalars, is known as a linear combination of the vectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\).

. . .

Definition 1.5: Span of Vectors

The span of a finite collection of vectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k \in \mathbb{R}^n\) is the subset \(V=\operatorname{span}\left\{\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) consisting of all possible linear combinations for \(c_1, \ldots, c_k \in \mathbb{R}\).

Linear Algebra Definitions (contd.)

Proposition 1.6: Span is a Subspace

The span of any collection of vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a subspace.

. . .

Definition 1.9: Linear Dependence and Independence

The vectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k \in \mathbb{R}^n\) are called linearly dependent if there exist scalars \(c_1, \ldots, c_k \in \mathbb{R}\), not all zero, such that

\[ c_1 \mathbf{v}_1+\cdots+c_k \mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{0} . \]

Vectors that are not linearly dependent are called linearly independent.

. . .

Lemma 1.11: Extending a Linear Independent Set

Let \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\) be linearly independent. If \(\mathbf{v}_{k+1} \notin \operatorname{span}\left\{\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\right\}\), then \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_{k+1}\) are also linearly independent.

. . .

Definition 1.12: Basis Vectors

A basis of a subspace \(V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) is a finite set of vectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k \in V\) that (a) spans \(V\), and (b) is linearly independent.

Application to Data Science

  • Suppose data in some subspace \(V\), and
  • A suitable basis \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\) exist for the data in \(V\).
  • Then the basis vectors span subspace \(V\)
  • Basis vectors provide a coordinate system for the subspace
  • Data can be represented in terms of basis vectors
  • Each data point is expressed as a linear combination of basis vectors
  • Linear combination coefficients represent the data points
  • Note: basis vectors are linearly independent but need not be orthogonal

Examples of Basis Vectors for Representing Data

  • Wavelet basis in signal processing
  • Fourier basis in frequency analysis
  • Polynomial basis in regression analysis
  • Principal component basis in PCA
  • Independent component basis in ICA
  • Non-negative basis in NMF
  • Each basis has unique properties suited for specific applications

. . .

Why do these basis vectors matter? How do we choose one set of basis vectors over another? What common characteristics do they share? What are the differences among them?

Dimension and Rank

Theorem 1.14: Dimension of a Subspace

Suppose the subspace \(V \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) has a basis \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k \in V\). Then every other basis of \(V\) has the same number, \(k\), of vectors in it. This number is called the dimension of \(V\), and written \(\operatorname{dim} V=k\). In particular, \(0<k \leq n\).

. . .

Lemma 1.17: Number of Vectors in a Spanning Set

Suppose \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\) span a subspace \(V \subset \mathbb{R}^n\). Then every set of \(m>k\) vectors \(\mathbf{w}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{w}_m \in V\) is linearly dependent.

. . .

Proposition 1.18: Rank

The vectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_k\) form a basis of a subspace \(V \subset \mathbb{R}^n\) if and only if every \(\mathbf{x} \in V\) can be written uniquely as a linear combination of the basis vectors: \[ \mathbf{x}=c_1 \mathbf{v}_1+\cdots+c_k \mathbf{v}_k=\sum_{i=1}^k c_i \mathbf{v}_i . \]

Gaining Intuition about Dimension and Rank

Suppose my data exist in some subspace V. Explain to me the relevance of the following result: e.g., Lemma 1.17.

  • If you collect 100 observations (\(m=100\)) but they all live in a 3-dimensional subspace (\(k=3\)), this theorem guarantees that at least 97 of those observations are “summarizable” by the others.

  • You don’t have 100 unique pieces of information; you have 3 pieces of information repeated and combined in 100 different ways.

  • This is the theoretical basis for Dimensionality Reduction. If you know your data is confined to a small \(k\), you can safely “compress” your \(m\) vectors down to \(k\) without losing any structural information.

. . .

Exercise: use an LLM to understand the implication of Theorem 1.14 in context of different basis vectors.

Theorem 1.19: Summary of Results for \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
  1. Every set of more than \(n\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is linearly dependent.
  2. No set of fewer than \(n\) vectors spans \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
  3. A set of \(n\) vectors forms a basis if and only if it spans \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
  4. A set of \(n\) vectors forms a basis if and only if it is linearly independent.

. . .

Proposition 1.21: Dimension of Subspaces

If \(W \subseteq V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) are subspaces, then \(0 \leq \operatorname{dim} W \leq \operatorname{dim} V \leq n\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{dim} V=\operatorname{dim} W\) if and only if \(V=W\).

. . .

Applying Linear Algebra to Representing Data

  • Data matrices can be viewed as collections of vectors in high-dimensional space
  • Test scores data: each student’s scores form a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^5\)
  • Linear combinations of basis vectors can represent data points
  • PCA components serve as orthogonal basis vectors
  • 5 components span the entire space \(\mathbb{R}^5\)
  • All rows can be expressed as linear combinations of 5 basis vectors (exact representation when using all 5 components)

Definition: Image of a Matrix

Let \(A=\left(\mathbf{v}_1 \ldots \mathbf{v}_n\right)\) be an \(m \times n\) matrix, whose columns \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n\) form a set of \(n\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^m\). The subspace spanned by its column vectors is known as the image of \(A\), and denoted \[ \operatorname{img} A=\operatorname{span}\left\{\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}^m . \]

Alternative names appearing in the literature include column space and range. Equivalently, the image of \(A\) can be defined as

\[ \operatorname{img} A=\left\{A \mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}^m . \]

We conclude that a vector \(\mathbf{b}\) lies in the image of \(A\) if and only if the linear system \(A \mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}\) has a solution.

. . .

Definition: Kernel of a Matrix

The kernel or, alternatively, null space of \(A\) is denoted by

\[ \operatorname{ker} A=\left\{\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid A \mathbf{z}=\mathbf{0}\right\} \subset \mathbb{R}^n . \]

The kernel is the set of solutions \(\mathbf{z}\) to the homogeneous linear system \(A \mathbf{z}=\mathbf{0}\).

Definition 3.6: Rank of a Matrix

The rank of a matrix \(A\) is the dimension of its image:

\[ \operatorname{rank} A=\operatorname{dim}\operatorname{img} A . \]

Definition 3.8: Nullity of a Matrix

The nullity of a matrix \(A\) is the dimension of its kernel:

\[ \operatorname{ nullity } A=\operatorname{dim} \operatorname{ker} A \text {. } \]

Theorem 3.9: Rank and Nullity of a Matrix

Let \(A\) be an \(m \times n\) matrix. Then

\[ \operatorname{rank} A+\text { nullity } A=n . \]

Rank Factorization of Matrices

Example: Matrix as a Sum of Rank-One Matrices

An \(m \times n\) matrix \(A\) has \(\operatorname{rank} A=1\) if and only if there are nonzero vectors \(\mathbf{0} \neq \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^m, \mathbf{0} \neq \mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^n\), such that \(A=\mathbf{v} \mathbf{w}^T\). More generally, we have \(\operatorname{rank} A=r>0\) if and only if there exist linearly independent vectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_r \in \mathbb{R}^m\), \(\mathbf{w}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{w}_r \in \mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(A\) can be expressed as a sum of \(r\) rank one matrices,

\[ A=\mathbf{v}_1 \mathbf{w}_1^T+\cdots+\mathbf{v}_r \mathbf{w}_r^T=V W^T, \]

where the matrices \(V=\left(\mathbf{v}_1 \ldots \mathbf{v}_r\right) \in \mathcal{M}_{m \times r}, W=\left(\mathbf{w}_1 \ldots \mathbf{w}_r\right) \in \mathcal{M}_{n \times r}\) with the indicated columns both have rank \(r\). Moreover, the vectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_r\) form a basis for \(\operatorname{img} A=\operatorname{img} V\).

PCA as a Rank Factorization of Data Matrix

Suppose test scores \(\mathbf{X}\) is represented as a sum of rank-one matrices \[ \mathbf{X}=q_1v_1^\top + \cdots + q_r v_r^\top = \sum_{k=1}^r \mathbf{Q}_k \mathbf{V}_k^T = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{V}^T \] where \(\mathbf{q}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{q}_r\) are \(n\)-dimensional vectors and \(\mathbf{v}_1, \cdots, \mathbf{v}_r\) are \(p\)-dimensional vectors for \(k=1, \ldots, r\). Rank \(r\) has a maximum of \(\min(n, p)=5\)2.

. . .

Is the decomposition into rank one matrices obvious in the way we think about matrix multiplication?

Matrix Multiplication: Elements of \(\boldsymbol{C}\)

Let \(\boldsymbol{C}\) be an \(m \times n\) matrix.

The \((i, j)\)-th element of the matrix product \(\boldsymbol{C}=\boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{B}\) is given by \[C_{i j}=A_{i\bullet} \cdot B_{\bullet j}\]

Matrix Multiplication: Rows of \(\boldsymbol{C}\)

Let \(\boldsymbol{C}\) be an \(m \times n\) matrix.

The \(i\)-th row of the matrix product \(\boldsymbol{C}=\boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{B}\) is given by \[C_{i \bullet}=A_{i\bullet} \cdot B\]

Matrix Multiplication: Columns of \(\boldsymbol{C}\)

Let \(\boldsymbol{C}\) be an \(m \times n\) matrix.

The \(j\)-th column of the matrix product \(\boldsymbol{C}=\boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{B}\) is given by

\[C_{\bullet j}=A \cdot B_{\bullet j}\]

Matrix Multiplication: \(\boldsymbol{C}=\boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{B}\)

Let \(\boldsymbol{C}\) be an \(m \times n\) matrix.

The matrix product \(\boldsymbol{C}=\boldsymbol{A} \boldsymbol{B}\) is given by \[C=\sum_{k=1}^K A_{\bullet k} \cdot B_{k \bullet}\]
